newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-SENNA DEATH PROMPTED SAFER RACING, SAYS HILL.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-SENNA DEATH PROMPTED SAFER RACING, SAYS HILL.

text.p: World champion Damon Hill said on Wednesday the death of Ayrton Senna in 1994 had prompted improvements in safety in Grand Prix motor racing.

Speaking on the eve of the trial at which his former team chief Frank Williams and five others face manslaughter charges in Italy over Senna's death in the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix, Hill said he felt the sport had progressed because of the tragedies of that weekend.
Senna was killed while leading during the opening laps of the race while Austrian Roland Ratzenberger, a friend of Hill's, had been killed during qualifying the previous day.
Hill spoke at Silverstone where he has been testing with his Arrows Yamaha team in preparation for the new Formula One season which opens in Melbourne, Australia, on March 9.
He said he had originally expected to be in Italy for the opening of the trial on Thursday but had been told he was no longer required.
He said he now expected to appear as a witness later in the year, probably shortly after this year's San Marino Grand Prix at Imola on April 27.
Hill said he did not relish being asked to recall the events of that tragic weekend which saw Ratzenberger and Senna killed.
"It's a very unpleasant thing to have to go through," he said. "It's bad enough the first time, but it's the requirement of the Italian law so we have to respect it.
"It's certainly not something I want to dwell on. But there are lessons to be learned and a lot has changed since Ayrton's death to make Formula One safer.
"But it will never be totally safe. If we had not changed things, as we have done, it would have been amiss of us -- especially if we had just carried on as before."

Asked about recent claims made by his former Williams team mate Jacques Villeneuve of Canada that Formula One was in danger of making itself too safe for its own good as a spectacle, he said: "This is not the right way of putting it."
He added: "We must continue to try and make it as safe as we can. We have got a responsibility to the sport and to the viewers of the sport to provide entertainment and not just a macabre spectacle.
"The safer it gets, the better the racing gets -- people feel more confident and take more liberties. And that improves the show for everyone."
